memory_update.text: AI theme should be mapped as a physical infrastructure stack: hyperscaler demand -> accelerators/custom ASICs -> foundry -> advanced packaging -> substrates/ABF film/HBM -> board power/passives -> optics/networking -> server/rack integration -> data-center power/grid.

Highest-priority Layer 2A bottlenecks: advanced packaging capacity, leading-edge foundry allocation, ABF substrates, ABF film, data-center electrical equipment, high-end MLCCs, and optical interconnect assembly/test.

Do not let GPU mega-cap narratives dominate the AI chain map; use NVIDIA and other AI accelerator leaders as demand anchors while searching for hidden value in substrates, materials, optics, EMS, passives, electrical equipment, and certification gates.
Broadcom-style disclosures on custom AI accelerators and AI networking are key catalysts for validating the custom ASIC inference lane and its dependence on TSMC capacity and advanced packaging.
Customer advance payments to substrate suppliers are a strong signal of substrate scarcity and should be tracked as a hard-evidence catalyst.
Switchgear, transformer, and medium-voltage equipment capacity expansion announcements are direct catalysts for the AI power-infrastructure bottleneck.

Need primary-source verification from latest filings, earnings calls, and investor decks for optical names including Fabrinet, Lumentum, Coherent, Applied Optoelectronics, Jabil, Sanmina, and Celestica.

Need primary-source checks for Murata, SEMCO, Taiyo Yuden, and other passive-component suppliers to verify AI-server MLCC revenue contribution, high-end capacity utilization, and whether margins show scarcity.
Need to verify ABF substrate claims against Ibiden, Shinko, Unimicron, Nan Ya PCB, AT&S, Ajinomoto, and customer filings or capex disclosures before ranking securities in later layers.
Need to separate regulated grid constraints from electrical-equipment supplier upside: utility interconnection delays may validate the bottleneck but can also delay data-center revenue conversion.

FN should be tracked as an underfollowed AI optical interconnect EMS/yield-learning candidate; promotion requires primary-source confirmation of datacom mix, 800G/1.6T exposure, customer concentration, and capacity constraints.
MRAAY should be tracked as an underfollowed AI-server passive-component bottleneck candidate, specifically for high-end MLCC intensity in AI servers and racks rather than generic MLCC exposure.

AVGO remains a reference-leader ticker for custom AI accelerators and AI networking demand, useful for validating whether hyperscaler inference and networking demand is propagating into second-order suppliers.

LITE and COHR are reference photonics names for AI datacenter optics, but Layer 2B should not assume scarcity economics until primary-source evidence separates AI datacenter demand from telecom, industrial, and cyclical recovery effects.

AAOI is an underfollowed optical-module candidate with potentially high AI datacenter sensitivity, but it requires stricter verification of 800G order durability, hyperscaler concentration, manufacturing yields, and margin quality.

JBL and SANM are second-order EMS/manufacturing hypotheses for AI optics and high-speed networking; both need materiality checks before promotion because diversified EMS labels can hide or dilute the actual AI exposure.
ALMU belongs only in the speculative-shadow lane until evidence shows datacenter customer traction, qualified manufacturing, production orders, cash runway, and optical-interconnect revenue.
The candidate chunk is truncated after Celestica; recover the full Layer 1 records before finalizing the ticker relationship map for CLS and any omitted candidates.
Need current market-cap and liquidity checks for every candidate because several cached market_cap_bucket labels may be stale or inconsistent with the underfollowed discovery lens.
Need primary-source filings, earnings transcripts, investor decks, product datasheets, and customer disclosures for all non-AVGO and non-MRAAY claims before Layer 3 promotion.
TSM is the strongest reference relationship in this chunk: leading-edge foundry plus CoWoS/SoIC advanced packaging directly maps to the AI accelerator capacity bottleneck.
ETN is the best-supported power-infrastructure reference relationship: supplied evidence directly links its U.S. medium-voltage switchgear production increase to data-center demand.
POWL is the highest-priority underfollowed power-infrastructure hypothesis, but it requires primary-source validation of data-center backlog and AI materiality before promotion.
MOD and NVT are adjacent data-center infrastructure hypotheses; both need quantified data-center revenue, AI order growth, backlog duration, and product-level exposure checks.

UCTT and MKSI are underfollowed semiconductor equipment-subsystem hypotheses tied to AI capacity expansion, but current evidence only supports node-level logic rather than company-specific AI revenue exposure.
AEHR and WOLF should remain speculative-shadow candidates until direct AI customer, qualification, backlog, revenue contribution, and balance-sheet evidence is found.

For every underfollowed name in this chunk, Layer 2C should collect primary-source filings and transcripts to distinguish real AI data-center exposure from generic industrial, semiconductor, or electrification cycles.

Need current market-cap, liquidity, short interest, valuation, and analyst-coverage checks to confirm which candidates still fit the underfollowed USD 300M-10B discovery lane and which have already been repriced as crowded AI infrastructure trades.

CSCO is a reference-lane AI networking and optical ecosystem ticker, not an underfollowed Serenity candidate. Use it to validate supplier pull-through into optical modules, photonics components, EMS/test, and AI Ethernet networking.

Need Cisco primary-source evidence: FY2026 filings, latest earnings transcript, investor deck, AI networking product roadmap, and management commentary quantifying AI infrastructure orders or revenue.

Need Cisco optical supplier mapping: Acacia/internal optics exposure, pluggable versus CPO roadmap, 800G/1.6T attach rates, supplier concentration, and named relationships with optical EMS or photonics vendors.
Need to test whether Cisco AI networking demand is additive to underfollowed suppliers or whether hyperscalers bypass Cisco through direct sourcing, white-box systems, or merchant silicon platforms.

Potential read-through tickers to investigate in later Layer 2 passes include optical EMS, photonics component, and module suppliers, but each must be promoted only after primary-source customer, revenue, or qualification evidence is found.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. AI industry-chain map for Serenity Layer 2A: the clearest chokepoint clusters are not only the high-attention GPU layer, but the physical scaling layers underneath it: leading-edge foundry allocation, advanced packaging such as CoWoS/SoIC, ABF substrates and ABF film, high-end MLCC/passive power components, high-speed optical interconnect manufacturing, and data-center electrical infrastructure. The near-term catalysts cluster around hyperscaler capex, custom AI ASIC ramp, packaging capacity additions, power-grid equipment orders, AI-server component intensity, and earnings disclosures that confirm whether scarcity is showing up in revenue, backlog, advance payments, lead times, or margins.

supply_chain_map.node: Hyperscaler AI demand and capex
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Cloud providers and large model operators drive the entire chain through GPU clusters, custom ASIC inference deployments, AI networking, and data-center buildouts. This is the root demand node that validates whether downstream bottlenecks are structural or cyclical.

supply_chain_map.node: AI accelerators and GPU platforms
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: High-attention reference layer that sets the bill-of-materials pull for HBM, substrates, advanced packaging, optics, power delivery, and passive components. It should be used as a demand anchor, not allowed to dominate the whole map.

supply_chain_map.node: Custom AI ASICs for hyperscaler inference
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Inference scaling appears to be shifting part of demand from generic GPU clusters toward hyperscaler-specific accelerators and networking silicon. This creates a separate capacity lane gated by leading-edge foundry, packaging, and networking supply.

supply_chain_map.node: Leading-edge foundry allocation
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Advanced AI accelerators and custom ASICs require leading-edge wafer capacity. If wafer allocation at TSMC or equivalent suppliers is tight, downstream AI deployments are capped even when demand is available.

supply_chain_map.node: Advanced packaging: CoWoS, SoIC, EMIB, Foveros and package test flows
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI chips increasingly require advanced packaging to combine logic, HBM, interposers, and high-bandwidth interconnect. Tool acceptance cycles, cleanroom buildouts, yield learning, and package-test capacity make this a slow-scaling physical chokepoint.

supply_chain_map.node: Advanced packaging equipment and cleanroom buildout
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Packaging capacity cannot be added instantly; equipment delivery, installation, cleanroom readiness, and qualification cycles can stretch across quarters. This creates second-order opportunities around tools, process equipment, inspection, and OSAT capacity.

supply_chain_map.node: ABF substrates for high-end AI packages
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Each AI chip generation tends to require larger, more complex substrates with more layers, finer features, and embedded power-delivery requirements. The supplier base narrows as complexity rises, making qualified substrate makers potential hidden chokepoints.

supply_chain_map.node: ABF film supply
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Advanced substrate makers depend on scarce ABF film. If allocation is tight, even well-funded substrate capacity additions can be constrained by material access. This is a low-attention material gate beneath AI accelerators.

supply_chain_map.node: HBM and memory stack integration
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: HBM is central to AI accelerator performance and also increases pressure on advanced packaging, substrate, and test flows. It is highly visible, so Layer 2A should treat it as important but not necessarily underfollowed.

supply_chain_map.node: High-end MLCCs and passive power components
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI servers require far more high-performance capacitors than standard servers because accelerator power transients demand lower impedance, low ESR, low ESL, and compact high-capacitance components. The chokepoint is the narrow high-end MLCC band, not commodity MLCCs.

supply_chain_map.node: Board-level power delivery and voltage regulation
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: As accelerator power density rises, boards need more sophisticated power stages, voltage regulators, capacitors, inductors, connectors, and thermal-aware layouts. This is a second-order AI infrastructure chain often hidden inside broad electronics categories.

supply_chain_map.node: Optical interconnects: 800G, 1.6T, CPO and silicon photonics
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI clusters create high east-west traffic, raising demand for high-speed optics. The bottleneck can shift from module demand to manufacturable photonics components, compound semiconductor capacity, assembly yield, and qualified test capacity.

supply_chain_map.node: Photonics components and InP-related capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: EMLs, lasers, photodetectors, pump lasers, silicon photonics components, and InP-related devices can become scarce as data-center optical speeds rise. Low-attention niche photonics suppliers may hide value if they control yield or capacity.

supply_chain_map.node: Optical module assembly, EMS, and test capacity
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Even when photonics designs exist, scaling 800G and 1.6T modules requires qualified precision manufacturing, assembly, and testing. This node can hide under broad EMS labels rather than obvious AI labels.

supply_chain_map.node: High-speed networking ASICs and switches
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI clusters need networking silicon and switching systems alongside accelerators. Custom silicon and AI networking growth can validate whether AI demand is moving from isolated GPU nodes into full-cluster infrastructure.

supply_chain_map.node: Connectors, cabling, and signal-integrity components
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Dense AI racks and scale-out networks require more copper, optical, and board-level interconnect products. This is often embedded in diversified interconnect companies, making exposure harder to screen.

supply_chain_map.node: AI server manufacturing and rack integration
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Server ODMs, EMS providers, rack integrators, and liquid-cooled system assemblers convert chips into deployable infrastructure. Bottlenecks may emerge in qualified manufacturing, thermal integration, and large-scale deployment logistics.

supply_chain_map.node: Data-center electrical equipment: medium-voltage switchgear, transformers, UPS, power distribution
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI clusters require large power additions. Medium-voltage equipment, switchgear, transformers, and skilled electrical labor are slow to expand and can delay data-center energization even when compute hardware is available.

supply_chain_map.node: Utility interconnection, grid access, and power permits
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Permitting, interconnection queues, utility capacity, and local grid constraints can become non-semiconductor bottlenecks. This node is regulated and location-specific, so it may create regional winners and losers.

supply_chain_map.node: Cooling infrastructure and thermal management
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Higher rack density increases demand for liquid cooling, heat exchangers, pumps, CDUs, cold plates, and facility-level thermal engineering. This is a likely adjacent bottleneck, but evidence in the supplied context is weaker than for packaging, substrates, MLCCs, and power equipment.
